scenes.heading: The cell cycle
scenes.sub: How cells copy themselves, and what keeps them in check
scenes.say: Your body makes millions of new cells every second. Too little division, and tissues can't repair. Too much, and a tumour can form. So how is it controlled?

scenes.heading: Interphase is not a rest
points: G1: the cell grows and does its job
G2: grows more and checks the DNA
scenes.say: Interphase is not a rest. In G one, the cell grows. In S phase, the DNA is copied, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids. In G two, the cell grows and checks the copies. Then comes M phase: mitosis and cytokinesis.
scenes.caption: Interphase is not a rest. In G1, the cell grows. In S phase, the DNA is copied, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids. In G2, the cell grows and checks the copies. Then comes M phase: mitosis and cytokinesis.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Copy every handout, line up the pairs, split them, file two sets
scenes.science: Mitosis gives two identical sets of chromosomes
scenes.breaks: Spindle fibres do the pulling, and the copying happens earlier, in interphase, not during mitosis.
scenes.say: Imagine a teacher making two identical sets of handouts. She copies every page and staples each pair, lines the pairs up down the desk, then unstaples them and slides one copy to each end. That's mitosis. But in a cell, spindle fibres do the pulling, and the copying happens earlier, in interphase.

scenes.heading: The stages of mitosis
steps: Metaphase: line up in the middle
scenes.say: Remember PMAT. In prophase, chromosomes appear. In metaphase, they line up in the middle. In anaphase, sister chromatids are pulled apart. In telophase, two nuclei form. Then cytokinesis splits the cell.

scenes.heading: Checkpoints and apoptosis
points: Can't fix it? Apoptosis: tidy cell death
scenes.say: Checkpoints are like the checks before a flight. At G one, the cell checks its size and DNA. At G two, it checks the copies. At M, it checks every chromosome is attached to the spindle. If damage can't be fixed, the cell goes into apoptosis: tidy, programmed cell death.
scenes.caption: Checkpoints are like the checks before a flight. At G1, the cell checks its size and DNA. At G2, it checks the copies. At M, it checks every chromosome is attached to the spindle. If damage can't be fixed, the cell goes into apoptosis: tidy, programmed cell death.

scenes.heading: Cancer: when control fails
scenes.say: Cancer starts with mutations in genes that control the cycle. A mutated proto-oncogene, called an oncogene, is like an accelerator stuck down. A mutated tumour suppressor gene, like the one for p fifty-three, is like brakes that have failed.
scenes.caption: Cancer starts with mutations in genes that control the cycle. A mutated proto-oncogene, called an oncogene, is like an accelerator stuck down. A mutated tumour suppressor gene, like the one for p53, is like brakes that have failed.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Of 200 onion root tip cells, 180 are in interphase. The cycle takes 24 hours. How long is interphase?
lines: Fraction of cells = fraction of time
scenes.say: Of two hundred onion root tip cells, one hundred and eighty are in interphase. The cycle takes twenty-four hours. The fraction of cells in a stage matches the fraction of time. Zero point nine times twenty-four gives twenty-one point six hours.
scenes.caption: Of 200 onion root tip cells, 180 are in interphase. The cycle takes 24 hours. The fraction of cells in a stage matches the fraction of time. 0.90 × 24 gives 21.6 hours.

points: Checkpoints at G1, G2 and M
scenes.say: Quick recap. Interphase has G one, S and G two. Mitosis is PMAT, then cytokinesis. Checkpoints keep the cycle safe, and apoptosis removes damaged cells. Cancer happens when control genes mutate. Now try the practice questions!
